articles.title: Vijay government may privatise TN's liquor sales to curb graft
articles.description: An intensified DVAC probe into a multi-crore liquor scam, allegedly involving former DMK Minister V Senthil Balaji, has led to a suggestion to privatise retail liquor sales in Tamil Nadu. The investigation targets alleged collusion in TASMAC bar licences, transport tenders, and procurement, with the Madras High Court dismissing Balaji's anticipatory bail plea. The FIR details systemic corruption, significant revenue loss, and illicit fund generation, prompting political reactions.

articles.title: HR&CE to route temple tenders through Tamil Nadu govt e-procurement portal
articles.description: All temples under HR&CE will now use the e-procurement portal for tenders. Standardized tender documents in Tamil and English will be used across all temples. Bidders can revise quotes below the base price, with contracts awarded to the lowest bidder. Revenue-generating temple auction rights will be granted for a two-year period. New norms aim to ensure transparency and encourage greater competition among bidders.

articles.title: TASMAC Scam Fallout: TVK Mulls Private Liquor Retail Under Strict Regulation
articles.description:
Chennai, Jul 30 (PTI) The DVAC's intensified probe in the multi-crore liquor scam, revealing a web of collusion allegedly involving former DMK Minister V Senthil Balaji, has sparked a suggestion to privatise retail sales in Tamil Nadu.

A source in the ruling Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) indicated that the government could give up its monopoly in the retail sales of liquor and allow private players keeping a strict hold on them through policy changes.

This suggestion has emerged with the DVAC tightening on Senthil Balaji in the liquor scam over an alleged collusion in issuing TASMAC bar licences, transport tenders, procurement and bottling operations between 2021 and 2025 during the DMK regime.

The investigation targets a web of senior politicians, state bureaucrats, distilleries and bottling operations accused of manipulating tenders and siphoning cash.

Incidentally, the Madras High Court on Thursday dismissed the anticipatory bail plea of Balaji in the corruption case, saying custodial interrogation is very much necessary.

On July 29, the Directorate of Vigilance and Anti-Corruption initiated simultaneous searches in nearly 45 locations across the state targeting the properties of Senthil Balaji and the agency formally registered a FIR naming him, former Tamil Nadu State Marketing Corporation Ltd (TASMAC) managing director S Visakan, senior regional managers and associates. They have been booked for collusion and malpractices spanning from 2021 to 2025.

The Enforcement Directorate and DVAC allege that a systematic framework was resorted to for generating massive illicit funds to the tune of Rs 1,000 crore over inflated operational expenses, fabricated purchases and securing higher liquor supply orders from the state-run liquor retailer TASMAC.

According to the FIR which named seven persons including Senthil Balaji, formerly Minister for Electricity, Prohibition, and Excise, the case was registered against them for allegations of misappropriation and manipulation of procurement and tender processes in allotting bar licences, transport tenders and bogus / inflated transactions by certain distilleries/breweries, transport firms and bottling firms / companies.

TASMAC operates around 5,380 liquor selling retail shops and 3,240 bars in the state. Its district managers are authorised to invite fresh tenders for running bars and selling of empty carton boxes. The revenue to the government from the sale at the retail shops had drastically increased year after year but in contrast, the revenue to government from TASMAC bars had drastically decreased.

During 2021 in Coimbatore, Nilgiris, Tirupur, Erode, Namakkal and Karur districts tenders were invited from public for 857 bars and the tender bid was opened on December 31, 2021 and finalised. The district managers "violated and breached the tender rules by allowing particular participants and extended favour to them," the FIR stated.

"The tenderers who participated in the tender process formed syndicate with themselves and submitted Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) Demand Draft from the same bank with continuous serial numbers which clearly shows that cartelisation had taken place in the above tenders," the FIR said.

In the said districts out of 857 bars, 284 were closed but in reality, these 284 bars still operated without renewal of the license. As per Government instruction, any bar not submitting the monthly Demand Draft, should be closed and fresh tender should be floated for the said bar. As the district managers of TASMAC and other officials colluded with the bar owners and did not follow the rules, it resulted in revenue loss to the government to the tune of Rs 17.27 crore in Coimbatore North, Rs.13.58 crore in Coimbatore South district and Rs 1.95 crore in Nilgiris district during 2022 - 2023, it said.

Further, it noted that annually TASMAC paid Rs 100 crore approximately to the transporters. Also, the old/used bottle suppliers had generated cash by supplying bogus invoices or inflating the invoice amount and receiving the payment from distilleries companies, after deducting their commission, they returned the cash amount to respective distilleries. In turn these distilleries used the said cash to provide the kickbacks to the officials for securing the supply orders.

It also found that TASMAC shops collected an excess amount than the actual MRP rate i.e. collecting up to Rs 500 excess for foreign liquor and depending upon the brand of the liquor Rs 10 to Rs 100 was illegally collected from the customer between 2021 to 2025 in an organised manner.

The alarming proportions of the liquor scam in the state made the AIADMK general secretary Edappadi K Palaniswami dub Senthil Balaji as "Rs 10 minister" during his political speeches. The moniker became a prominent political weapon with even TVK chief C Joseph Vijay labelling him as "ten rupees minister." A source in the TVK said the government should pursue its mission to eradicate corruption and plug the leakages. It could allow private players to run the shops under strict government vigilance.

(Disclaimer: This report has been published as part of the auto-generated syndicate wire feed. Apart from the headline, no editing has been done in the copy by ABP Live.)

articles.title: MSME Amendment Bill 2026: Delayed Payments, MSEFCs and Key Reforms Explained
articles.description: Introduced in Rajya Sabha, the proposed legislation seeks stronger enforcement of arbitral awards, faster resolution of payment disputes and greater flexibility for states to establish MSME Facilitation Councils India’s proposed overhaul of its principal MSME law has entered Parliament at a particularly consequential moment for the country’s small-business economy. Union Minister for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Jitan Ram Manjhi introduced the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development (Amendment) Bill, 2026 in the Rajya Sabha on July 28, 2026. The Bill seeks to amend the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006, with a strong focus on delayed payments, enforcement of arbitral awards, ease of doing business and expansion of the dispute-resolution infrastructure available to micro and small enterprises. The introduction took place during the Monsoon Session of Parliament, scheduled from July 20 to August 13, 2026, with 19 sittings. The MSME Amendment Bill is among five new Bills listed by the government for introduction, consideration and passage during the session. Ref: PRS Legislative Research While the detailed clause-by-clause implications will become clearer through parliamentary consideration, the stated objectives suggest that the government is attempting to correct one of the biggest weaknesses of the existing MSME framework: a legal right to timely payment that has often proved difficult to enforce in practice. Why the MSMED Act, 2006 Needs an Upgrade The MSMED Act, 2006 was a landmark law because it gave formal statutory recognition to micro, small and medium enterprises as a distinct economic category. It also introduced specific protections for micro and small enterprises against delayed payments. However, the commercial environment in which MSMEs operate has changed dramatically during the last two decades. Digital procurement, platform-based commerce, GST -linked invoicing, electronic marketplaces, fintech-based lending, supply-chain financing and online dispute resolution have transformed business transactions. At the same time, small suppliers continue to face old problems: unequal bargaining power, delayed invoices, expensive litigation and dependence on a few large customers. The new Bill seeks to align the 2006 law with this changing MSME landscape, enhance ease of doing business and introduce what the government describes as a more “trust-based” regulatory environment. That language is significant. Trust-based regulation should ideally mean simpler compliance for genuine enterprises, but stronger accountability for buyers that deliberately retain payments owed to smaller suppliers. Delayed Payments Remain the Central Challenge Under the existing MSMED Act, a buyer is required to pay a micro or small enterprise within the period agreed between the parties. That agreed period cannot ordinarily exceed 45 days from the date of acceptance or deemed acceptance of the goods or services. If payment is delayed, the buyer becomes liable to pay compound interest with monthly rests at three times the bank rate notified by the Reserve Bank of India. On paper, this is a powerful protection. In practice, however, many small businesses do not receive either the principal amount or the statutory interest within a commercially meaningful period. The Ministry of MSME’s Annual Report 2025–26 reveals the scale of the problem. Up to December 31, 2025, micro and small enterprises had filed 2,56,892 delayed-payment applications involving ₹55,244.31 crore on the MSME Samadhaan platform. The report records that: 24,238 matters involving ₹3,018.37 crore were resolved through mutual settlement. 52,744 applications involving ₹8,397.25 crore were yet to be examined by the Facilitation Councils. 47,088 applications involving approximately ₹14,243 crore had been converted into cases. 53,911 cases involving ₹14,638.38 crore had been disposed of by MSEFCs. These numbers demonstrate both the value and limitations of the existing mechanism. Thousands of enterprises have been able to formally raise claims, but the volume of applications awaiting scrutiny or adjudication remains substantial. Ministry of MSME Annual Report 2025–26 The Economic Survey 2025–26, as cited in the Ministry’s annual report, estimated that approximately ₹8.1 lakh crore could be locked in delayed payments to MSMEs . This wider estimate goes far beyond the claims formally filed on government portals, suggesting that a large proportion of businesses either do not report their dues or do not initiate proceedings. Why Many MSMEs Do Not File Claims The delayed-payment crisis cannot be understood merely as a legal or administrative problem. It is also a question of commercial dependence. A small component manufacturer may depend on one large corporate customer for half of its annual turnover. A service provider may rely on a government department or public-sector company for repeat contracts. Filing a case against that buyer could help recover an old invoice but might also end the commercial relationship. This fear frequently discourages entrepreneurs from using the remedies available under the law. The Ministry’s Annual Report acknowledges this concern. It notes that an MSME filing a delayed-payment case may be perceived by the buyer as taking an adversarial position, potentially affecting future orders. Consequently, the most effective payment framework cannot rely only on litigation. It must combine preventive disclosure, digital payment tracking, mediation, conciliation, arbitration and enforceable consequences for habitual defaulters. What the MSME Amendment Bill 2026 Proposes The official legislative agenda identifies four broad objectives for the Bill. 1. Strengthening the Delayed-Payment Mechanism The Bill seeks to strengthen the system through which micro and small enterprises can pursue delayed-payment claims. This could potentially involve procedural changes intended to reduce bottlenecks between filing an application, registering it as a case, conducting conciliation, beginning arbitration and issuing an award. The effectiveness of this reform will depend on whether the final legislation creates clear timelines and accountability for every stage of the process. The existing law already envisages that a reference should be decided within 90 days. However, high case volumes, institutional shortages, adjournments and procedural disputes have often made this target difficult to achieve. A stronger law must therefore distinguish between a statutory aspiration and an enforceable case-management deadline. 2. Enforcement of Arbitral Awards One of the Bill’s most consequential objectives is to provide for the enforcement of arbitral awards in favour of micro and small enterprises. Winning an arbitration does not automatically put money into the supplier’s bank account. A successful enterprise may still face legal challenges, execution proceedings and further delays before recovering the award. For an MSME, this gap between obtaining an award and actually receiving the money can be financially devastating. The proposed enforcement provisions could become the Bill’s most transformative feature if they create a fast, digitally tracked and time-bound route from award to recovery. However, Parliament will need to examine how the new mechanism interacts with the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, particularly in relation to challenges against awards, execution jurisdiction and interim protection. The final system must protect legitimate rights of appeal without allowing the appellate process to become a strategy for indefinitely withholding payments. 3. Greater Flexibility for States to Constitute MSEFCs The Bill proposes to empower states to determine the composition of Micro and Small Enterprises Facilitation Councils. This is intended to help states establish more councils according to local caseloads and administrative requirements. At present, differences in institutional capacity across states affect the quality and speed of dispute resolution. A state with one overloaded council cannot provide the same access as a state operating multiple councils across different regions. Punjab, Maharashtra, Telangana, Odisha, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal and Delhi are among the jurisdictions that have established multiple MSEFCs, according to the Ministry’s annual report. Giving states greater flexibility could enable: District-level or regional Facilitation Councils. Sector-specific benches in high-volume industrial regions. More frequent hearings. Inclusion of members with commercial and technical experience. Special arrangements for remote and online hearings. Faster disposal of relatively small claims. Flexibility, however, must not come at the cost of independence or consistency. Minimum national standards will still be necessary for council composition, member qualifications, conflict-of-interest disclosures, digital case management and publication of performance data. 4. Ease of Doing Business and Trust-Based Regulation The government has also positioned the Bill as an ease-of-doing-business reform. For MSMEs, ease of doing business should not be measured only by the number of registrations or forms eliminated. It must also be measured by how quickly a lawful invoice is paid, how predictably a contract is enforced and how affordable it is for a small company to obtain justice. A supplier that waits nine months for payment is effectively financing the buyer’s business without consent. During this period, the supplier must still pay GST, salaries, rent, electricity charges, bank instalments and vendors. Therefore, payment discipline is itself an ease-of-doing-business issue. The Critical Link With MSME ODR The legislative reform comes alongside the government’s effort to expand online dispute resolution. All new delayed-payment cases have been directed to the MSME ODR Portal since October 15, 2025, with the platform being integrated with MSME Samadhaan. The ODR model encourages an amicable settlement before a dispute moves into formal conciliation or arbitration. The government has provided an outlay of ₹189 crore for the MSE Online Dispute Resolution scheme. The early results remain limited but instructive. According to the Annual Report 2025–26, the portal disposed of 17 cases during its initial eight months. Fifteen were resolved at the pre-MSEFC or amicable-settlement stage and two at the conciliation stage, resulting in settlements worth ₹60.60 lakh. The next challenge is scale. A platform processing a few dozen cases will not be sufficient when the existing ecosystem contains lakhs of applications and delayed dues potentially running into several lakh crore rupees. The amended law and the ODR platform must therefore operate as one integrated system rather than as separate policy initiatives. Will Medium Enterprises Receive Delayed-Payment Protection? Despite the full name of the MSMED Act covering micro, small and medium enterprises, the existing delayed-payment protections primarily apply to micro and small enterprises. Whether the 2026 amendments will extend some or all of these protections to medium enterprises will be an important point to watch as the Bill is debated and its final provisions are examined. Medium enterprises can also face severe payment pressure, particularly when supplying to large corporates, infrastructure companies, public-sector entities and government agencies. At the same time, lawmakers may need to consider whether extending the complete mechanism to medium enterprises could significantly increase the workload of already stretched Facilitation Councils. A calibrated approach could involve separate thresholds, benches or procedures for medium-enterprise claims. Until the final wording is adopted, businesses should not assume that every protection available to micro and small units will automatically apply to medium enterprises. What Parliament Should Examine The Bill’s objectives are directionally positive, but its ultimate impact will depend on operational detail. Parliament should closely examine the following issues: Automatic Recognition of Delayed Invoices Where invoices are digitally reported through GST systems, GeM, TReDS or government procurement portals, the framework should explore automatic identification of payments crossing the statutory limit. MSMEs should not always have to initiate a dispute before delayed payments become visible to regulators. Accountability for Habitual Defaulters The system should differentiate between a genuine commercial dispute and repeated withholding of undisputed invoices. Large buyers, government departments, public-sector enterprises and companies with a persistent history of delayed payments should face enhanced disclosure and monitoring requirements. Mandatory Buyer-Level Disclosure Companies should disclose the number and value of invoices owed to registered micro and small suppliers beyond the statutory period. This information should be presented in a consistent and machine-readable format. Time-Bound Enforcement A favourable award is of limited value if enforcement takes years. The amended framework must include clear execution timelines and narrowly defined grounds for delay. Protection Against Commercial Retaliation The law should consider mechanisms that protect suppliers from blacklisting or arbitrary exclusion merely because they invoked a statutory payment remedy. This is particularly important in government and public-sector procurement. Stronger Digital Integration Udyam, GSTN, GeM, TReDS, Samadhaan, the MSME ODR Portal and corporate disclosure systems should be interoperable, subject to appropriate privacy and cybersecurity safeguards. Public Performance Dashboards State-wise information should be published on: Applications received. Applications admitted. Settlement rates. Average disposal time. Awards issued. Awards enforced. Amounts recovered. Cases pending beyond prescribed timelines. Such disclosure would create accountability while helping states identify capacity gaps. What MSMEs Should Do Now Even a stronger law will benefit only those enterprises that maintain reliable documentation. MSMEs should immediately review their commercial and accounting practices. Purchase orders, delivery acknowledgements, invoices, email correspondence, payment terms and proof of acceptance should be properly preserved. Every invoice should correctly mention the enterprise’s Udyam registration details and clearly specify the payment period. Businesses should also reconcile Udyam, PAN, GST and bank information to avoid technical objections during dispute proceedings. Entrepreneurs should distinguish between disputed and undisputed invoices and begin payment follow-ups before the 45-day period expires. Where possible, they should consider invoice discounting through TReDS rather than waiting until a liquidity crisis emerges. Buyers Must Prepare for Greater Scrutiny The Bill is not relevant only for MSME suppliers. Large companies, public-sector enterprises, government departments and other institutional buyers must also examine their procurement and accounts-payable systems. Buyers should map all vendors registered as micro or small enterprises, identify invoices approaching the statutory deadline and establish internal escalation procedures. A procurement team that delays approval, a project manager who withholds a completion certificate or an accounts department that keeps an invoice pending for technical reasons could expose the organisation to substantial interest and legal liability. Companies must treat MSME payment compliance as a board-level governance and supply-chain resilience issue, rather than merely an accounts function. SMEStreet Perspective: Implementation Will Decide the Outcome The MSME Development Amendment Bill, 2026 represents an important acknowledgement that delayed payments cannot be addressed through portals and advisories alone. India already has a statutory payment period, penal interest provisions, Facilitation Councils and an online filing system. Yet vast sums remain locked outside the formal claims process, while thousands of filed applications await examination or resolution. The real test of the amended law will therefore not be whether it introduces another remedy. It will be whether it makes existing rights practically enforceable. If the Bill enables more Facilitation Councils, professionalises their functioning, integrates online dispute resolution and creates an effective route for enforcement of awards, it could materially improve working-capital conditions across the MSME economy. If implementation remains fragmented across states, however, the amendments could add another legal layer without substantially accelerating recovery. The opportunity before Parliament is bigger than procedural reform. India has an opportunity to transform timely payment from a contractual expectation into a measurable element of corporate accountability and responsible procurement. For millions of enterprises operating with limited cash reserves, that change could determine whether an order becomes a growth opportunity or a financial burden.
